title: Cap. VIII Arg. 1 Resp. coda (Vasquez): reprobates excluded from God himself without occasion from demerits
latin: Vasques Jesuita, qui nostrae defensioni non admodum favet, tamen hac in re nobis suffragatur: Ea gratia, inquit ille, peculiari et efficaci, quae est propria praedestinatorum, Deus absque dubio omnes reprobos ex seipso antecedente voluntate exclusit, nulla prorsus ex ipsis arrepta occasione. Negatio enim hujus gratiae nostram libertatem omnino praecedit. Hoc nobis perinde est ac si dixisset, Deum ex seipso, antecedente voluntate, nulla ex ipsorum demeritis arrepta occasione, omnes reprobos praeteriisse sive reprobasse.
pass_a: Vasquez the Jesuit, who does not greatly favor our defense, yet in this matter votes with us: By that peculiar and efficacious grace, says he, which is proper to the predestined, God without doubt excluded all the reprobate from himself by antecedent will, no occasion at all having been seized from them. For the negation of this grace altogether precedes our liberty. This is to us just as if he had said that God from himself, by antecedent will, no occasion having been seized from their demerits, passed by or reprobated all the reprobate.
pass_b: Vasquez the Jesuit — no great friend of our defense — still sides with us here. By that peculiar efficacious grace proper to the predestined, he says, God without doubt excluded all the reprobate from himself by antecedent will, seizing no occasion at all from them. Denial of that grace wholly precedes our liberty. For us that is as good as saying: God from himself, by antecedent will, with no occasion taken from their demerits, passed by or reprobated all the reprobate.

lemmas.gloss: Vasquez sides with us on antecedent exclusion
no occasion seized from reprobates' demerits

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 2: Rom. 9 — reprobation called hatred of Esau
latin: Secundo, conantur demonstrare praevisa demerita esse causam reprobationis (quod mirum alicui videri potest) ex ipsa disputatione Apostoli Rom. ix. Ubi nobis videtur contrariam sententiam stabilire. Primo ex eo quod Apostolus vocat hanc reprobationem odium; Esau odio habui: Deus autem neminem odit nisi peccati causa.
pass_a: Secondly, they try to demonstrate that foresighted demerits are the cause of reprobation (which may seem strange to someone) from the very disputation of the Apostle in Romans 9. Where it seems to us that he establishes the contrary opinion. First from this, that the Apostle calls this reprobation hatred; Esau I have hated: But God hates no one except for the cause of sin.
pass_b: Second, they try to prove foresighted demerits are the cause of reprobation — oddly enough — from Paul's own debate in Romans 9, where we take him to establish the opposite. First: the Apostle calls this reprobation hatred — Esau I hated — and God hates no one except for sin.

lemmas.gloss: Rom. 9: reprobation styled hatred of Esau
adversaries: God hates only for sin

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 2 Resp.: Paul removes good and evil acts; Augustine Contra 2 Epist. Pelag.
latin: Respondeo primo, illos directe impingere in mentem et clara verba Apostoli hac sua argutatione. Nam Paulus id agit hoc in loco, ut doceat electionem et rejectionem personarum singularium non pendere ex diversis aut contrariis actibus hominum, sed ex diverso Dei beneplacito volentis hujus misereri, illius non misereri. Atque hanc ob causam non modo removet bonas eorum actiones, sed etiam malas; Cum nondum nati fuissent, aut aliquid boni aut mali egissent. Quod autem ad eos attinet qui obtendunt Deum non spectasse quidem opera quae fecerunt, sed quae praevidit eos facturos, atque inde dilexisse Jacobum, et odisse Esavum, cum sint ipso Apostolo perspicaciores, qui hanc responsionem excogitare non potuit, ego eos non refellam, sed suo insomnia frui permittam. Id tantum monebo, Augustinum patienter audiant, qui hoc inepto effugio irritatus in haec verba prorupit: Profecto desipitis, qui dicente veritate, NON EX OPERIBUS, SED EX VOCANTE DICTUM EST, vos dicitis, ex futuris operibus quae Deus illum facturum esse praesciebat, Jacob fuisse dilectum, etc. Contr. 2. Epist. Pelag. lib. 2, cap. 7.
pass_a: I answer first that they by this their argumentation directly strike against the mind and clear words of the Apostle. For Paul in this place does this, that he may teach that the election and rejection of singular persons do not hang upon diverse or contrary acts of men, but upon the diverse good pleasure of God willing to have mercy on this one, not to have mercy on that one. And for this cause he removes not only their good actions, but also their evil ones; When they had not yet been born, or had done anything good or evil. But as to those who pretend that God did not indeed regard the works which they did, but those which he foresaw they would do, and thence loved Jacob and hated Esau — since they are more perspicacious than the Apostle himself, who could not invent this response — I will not refute them, but will permit them to enjoy their dream. This only I will warn, that they patiently hear Augustine, who, irritated by this inept escape, broke forth into these words: Truly you dote, who, when the truth says, NOT OF WORKS, BUT OF HIM THAT CALLETH, you say that from future works which God foresaw he would do, Jacob was loved, etc. Against two Letters of the Pelagians, book 2, chapter 7.
pass_b: First reply: their argument strikes straight against Paul's mind and plain words. In this place he teaches that election and rejection of particular persons do not hang on diverse or contrary human acts, but on God's diverse good pleasure — willing to have mercy on one, not on another. For that cause he removes not only their good acts but their evil ones: when they were not yet born, nor had done anything good or evil. As for those who claim God regarded not works done but works he foresaw they would do — and so loved Jacob and hated Esau — since they are sharper than the Apostle himself, who could not invent that answer, I will not refute them; let them enjoy their dream. Only this: hear Augustine patiently. Irritated by that inept escape he broke out: You truly dote who, when truth says NOT OF WORKS BUT OF HIM THAT CALLS, say Jacob was loved from future works God foresaw he would do (Against two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7).

lemmas.gloss: election/rejection from good pleasure, not acts

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 2 Resp.: demerit frees from cruelty charge, not motive of Jacob/Esau discrimination
latin: Porro et illud notandum est, nos libenter agnoscere, in subjecto reprobato residere illam contagionem et indignitatem quae possit Deum reprobantem non modo ab omni crudelitate et injustitia, sed vel a levissima ejus suspicione, liberare. Nam cuicunque negatur haec specialis misericordia, certum est, non habuisse illum jus ad hoc, quod gratia talis ei praeparetur aut conferatur. Rationabiliter autem negatur quod nulla ratione debetur, ut recte Thomas. Huc accedit, quod non modo nullum jus habet ad tale beneficium, sed est suo insito vitio quasi proxime dispositus ad vindictam Dei excipiendam. Hoc Augustinus optime explicavit, Contra 2. Epist. Pelag. lib. 2, cap. 7. Status enim totius generis humani Deo eligenti et praetereunti repraesentatus, est status peccati, status mortis et meritae damnationis. Verum cum hic status communis sit omnium, tamque Jacobum involvat quam Esavum, potest afferri ut ratio congrua cur Deus utrumque juste possit relinquere, sed non potest commode obtendi ut causa motiva cur Esavum rejecerit, electo Jacobo, qui in eadem fuit conditione. Atque hinc Dionysius Carthusianus intolerabile esse affirmat, ut praescientia demeritorum dicatur ratio reprobationis.
pass_a: Further this also is to be noted, that we gladly acknowledge that in the reprobated subject there resides that contagion and unworthiness which can free the reprobating God not only from all cruelty and injustice, but even from the lightest suspicion of it. For to whomsoever this special mercy is denied, it is certain that he had no right to this, that such grace should be prepared or conferred upon him. But what is owed by no reason is reasonably denied, as Thomas rightly. To this is added that he not only has no right to such a benefit, but by his inborn vice is as it were proximately disposed to receive the vengeance of God. This Augustine explained most well, Against two Letters of the Pelagians, book 2, chapter 7. For the state of the whole human race represented to God electing and passing by is a state of sin, a state of death and of merited damnation. But since this state is common to all, and involves Jacob as much as Esau, it can be brought forward as a congruent reason why God can justly leave both, but it cannot conveniently be pretended as the moving cause why he rejected Esau, Jacob having been elected, who was in the same condition. And hence Dionysius the Carthusian affirms it to be intolerable that foresight of demerits be called the reason of reprobation.
pass_b: Note also: we gladly grant that in the reprobate subject there resides that contagion and unworthiness which can free the reprobating God not only from cruelty and injustice, but even from the lightest suspicion of them. Whoever is denied this special mercy had no right that such grace be prepared or conferred. What is owed by no reason is reasonably denied — so Thomas. Add that he not only has no right to such a benefit, but by inborn vice is as it were proximately disposed to receive God's vengeance (Augustine, Against two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7). The state of the whole human race as presented to God electing and passing by is a state of sin, death, and merited damnation. But since that state is common to all and wraps Jacob as much as Esau, it can stand as a congruent reason why God may justly leave both — not as the moving cause why he rejected Esau while electing Jacob, who stood in the same condition. Hence Dionysius the Carthusian calls it intolerable that foresight of demerits be named the reason of reprobation.

lemmas.gloss: demerit frees God from cruelty charge
foresight of demerits not ratio of reprobation

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 2 Resp.: twofold hate — vengeance vs less love; Vasquez; Leah
latin: Postremo (quod directe nervos hujus argumenti elidit) dico Deum posse dici odisse Esavum duplici respectu: Vel odisse ad vindictam et poenam aeternae mortis illi infligendam: atque sic non odit Esavum nisi qua peccatorem, et propter ipsum peccatum, ut hujus odii causam motivam et demeritoriam: Vel odisse Esavum ad specialis alicujus et indebiti beneficii negationem, hoc est minus dilexisse: et sic potest odisse Esavum, tantum quia non vult eum diligere. Hoc sensu posteriore dicitur Deus ab Apostolo dilexisse Jacobum et odisse Esavum, quia pro liberrimo voluntatis suae proposito voluit Jacobum emollire per specialem gratiam; noluit autem hoc tanto beneficio afficere Esavum. Si hic quaeratur quare elegit Jacobum ad hanc specialem gratiam, et non Esavum, respondetur, Quia Deus sic voluit. Si cur quaeratur quare sic voluerit, stulta est quaestio, quia Divinae voluntatis in bonis suis gratuitis praeparandis et distribuendis quaeritur causa, cujus nulla est praeter suam causam. Jam vero quod odii vocabulum usurpatur pro sola negatione specialis amoris in speciali beneficio conferendo, non diffitentur ipsi Jesuitae. Vasques ad haec ipsa verba Apostoli respiciens, Odisse, inquit, idem est quod minus dilexisse. Habet enim se ad modum odientis, qui aliquod donum quod uni dat, alteri non concedit. Sic tale odisse non requirit peccatum ut causam hujus odii. Hoc sensu Jacob dicitur odio habuisse Leam, Gen. xxix. 31.
pass_a: Lastly (which directly breaks the nerves of this argument) I say that God can be said to have hated Esau in a twofold respect: Either to have hated unto vengeance and the punishment of eternal death to be inflicted upon him: and thus he does not hate Esau except as a sinner, and on account of the sin itself, as the moving and demeritorious cause of this hatred: Or to have hated Esau unto the negation of some special and unowed benefit, that is, to have loved less: and thus he can hate Esau only because he does not will to love him. In this latter sense God is said by the Apostle to have loved Jacob and hated Esau, because according to the freest purpose of his will he willed to soften Jacob by special grace; but he did not will to affect Esau with this so great benefit. If here it be asked why he chose Jacob unto this special grace, and not Esau, it is answered, Because God so willed. If it be asked why he so willed, the question is foolish, because a cause is sought of the Divine will in preparing and distributing its gratuitous goods, of which there is none besides its own cause. But now that the vocabulary of hatred is used for the mere negation of special love in conferring a special benefit, the Jesuits themselves do not deny. Vasquez, looking back to these very words of the Apostle, To hate, says he, is the same as to have loved less. For he bears himself after the manner of one hating, who does not grant to another some gift which he gives to one. Thus such hating does not require sin as the cause of this hatred. In this sense Jacob is said to have held Leah in hatred, Gen. 29:31.
pass_b: Lastly — and this breaks the nerve of the argument — God may be said to have hated Esau in two respects. First, hated unto vengeance and the punishment of eternal death: so he hates Esau only as a sinner, and for sin itself as moving and demeritorious cause. Second, hated unto denial of some special unowed benefit — that is, loved less: so he can hate Esau only because he does not will to love him. In that latter sense the Apostle says God loved Jacob and hated Esau: by the freest purpose of his will he chose to soften Jacob by special grace, and refused Esau that great benefit. Why choose Jacob for that grace and not Esau? Because God so willed. Why so will? A foolish question — you seek a cause of the divine will in preparing and distributing gratuitous goods beyond the will itself. That hatred here means mere denial of special love in conferring a special benefit, even the Jesuits grant. Vasquez on these very words: to hate is the same as to have loved less. He acts like one who hates who gives a gift to one and withholds it from another. Such hatred needs no sin as its cause. So Jacob is said to have hated Leah (Gen. 29:31).

lemmas.gloss: hate as vengeance vs hate as less love

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 3: hardening (Rom. 9) said to presuppose sins as motive of reprobation
latin: Apostolus vocat reprobationem: Miserebitur cujus vult, et quem vult indurat. Haec autem voluntas indurandi peccata reprobi, in quibus is induratur, praesupponit: Ergo peccata reproborum, cum quibus e vita hac decedunt, sunt causa motiva seu meritoria reprobationis eorundem.
pass_a: The Apostle calls reprobation: He will have mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens. But this will of hardening presupposes the sins of the reprobate, in which he is hardened: Therefore the sins of the reprobate, with which they depart from this life, are the moving or meritorious cause of the reprobation of the same.
pass_b: Third: the Apostle styles reprobation thus — He has mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens. But the will to harden presupposes the reprobate's sins in which he is hardened. Therefore the sins with which the reprobate leave this life are the moving or meritorious cause of their reprobation.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 3 Resp.: hardening is nolle misereri; foresight of final persistence not its cause
latin: Respondemus, hanc voluntatem indurandi, ab Apostolo eo in loco commemoratam, designare peculiarem actum Divinae voluntatis, secundum quem negat quibusdam personis singularem illam gratiam, qua corda illorum emollirentur. Deus enim, ut vere Augustinus, non obdurat impertundo malitiam, sed non impertundo misericordiam: sicut sol occidens radiosque suos retrahens dicatur aerem obtenebrare, non per influxum aliquem quo obtenebratio gignatur, sed per negationem ejus influxus, quo posito tenebrae tollerentur. Cum itaque haec obduratio fiat permittendo, et negando specialem misericordiam, manifestum est, non posse aliquem a Deo considerari et praevideri ut finaliter in peccatis suis obduratum et morientem, nisi praecedente decreto hujus permissivae obdurationis, vel hac negatione specialis misericordiae, qua novit Deus hanc in peccatis permansionem finalem impediendam fore, si concederetur. Quod igitur in argumento assumptum fuit, voluntatem hanc indurandi, quae reprobatio est, peccata reprobi praesupponere ut causam hujus reprobationis vel indurationis, non modo falsum est, sed a ratione et sensu communi alienum. Causa enim praecedit effectum suum: at haec finalis permansio reproborum in peccatis suis sequitur decretum illud non-miserendi sive indurandi. Nam si Deus miseretur, homo non induratur; ad hanc enim specialem misericordiam pertinet efficere ut emolliatur. Unde Augustinus: Si vellet Deus ipsorum misereri, posset ita vocare (quemadmodum illis aptum esset) ut et moverentur, et intelligerent, et sequerentur. Paulo post, Nullius Deus frustra miseretur. Tandem adjungit, Obdurationem Dei nihil aliud esse quam nolle misereri; scilicet appositione hujus gratiae infallibiliter et efficaciter hominem emollientis et convertentis. Cum igitur nulla finalis pertinacia cujusquam in peccatis contractis vel commissis supponi possit quam non praecedat voluntas Dei de non-emolliendo, praevisa reproborum perseverantia in peccatis suis non potest esse causa negatae hujus misericordiae aut emollitionis. Est illud quidem verum, in cursu vitae suae quotidiano, reprobos, extinguendo illud lumen quod Deus in illorum cordibus accendit, et repellendo motiones Divinas, atque turpiter parendo foedis libidinibus, mereri illam consequentem excaecationem, desertionem, et in reprobum sensum traditionem; Sed hisce omnibus praesupponitur permissio illa Divina, sive negatio gratiae specialis, quae induratio permissiva vocari potest, et a reprobatione dimanat, absque qua praeeunte, et ex liberrima Dei voluntate dependente, reprobi in praedictam finalem contumaciam non incidissent, sed specialis et indebitae misericordiae beneficio ab illa rebellione et duritia fuissent liberati.
pass_a: We answer that this will of hardening, commemorated by the Apostle in that place, designates a peculiar act of the Divine will, according to which he denies to certain persons that singular grace by which their hearts would be softened. For God, as Augustine truly, does not harden by imparting malice, but by not imparting mercy: as the setting sun, drawing back its rays, may be said to darken the air, not by some influx by which darkening is begotten, but by negation of that influx, which being posited darkness would be taken away. Since therefore this hardening is done by permitting, and by denying special mercy, it is manifest that no one can be considered and foresighted by God as finally hardened in his sins and dying, unless the decree of this permissive hardening, or this negation of special mercy, precede, by which God knows that this final remaining in sins would be impeded, if it were granted. What therefore was assumed in the argument, that this will of hardening, which is reprobation, presupposes the sins of the reprobate as the cause of this reprobation or hardening, is not only false, but alien from reason and common sense. For a cause precedes its effect: but this final remaining of the reprobate in their sins follows that decree of not-having-mercy or of hardening. For if God has mercy, man is not hardened; for it belongs to this special mercy to effect that he be softened. Whence Augustine: If God willed to have mercy on them, he could so call (as would be apt for them) that they would both be moved, and understand, and follow. A little after, God has mercy on no one in vain. At length he adds that the hardening of God is nothing other than not to will to have mercy; namely by the apposition of this grace infallibly and efficaciously softening and converting the man. Since therefore no final obstinacy of anyone in contracted or committed sins can be supposed which the will of God concerning not-softening does not precede, the foresighted perseverance of the reprobate in their sins cannot be the cause of this denied mercy or softening. That indeed is true, that in the daily course of their life the reprobate, by extinguishing that light which God kindles in their hearts, and by repelling Divine motions, and by basely obeying foul lusts, merit that consequent blinding, desertion, and handing over unto a reprobate sense; But to all these is presupposed that Divine permission, or negation of special grace, which can be called permissive hardening, and flows from reprobation, without which going before, and depending from the freest will of God, the reprobate would not have fallen into the aforesaid final contumacy, but by the benefit of special and unowed mercy would have been freed from that rebellion and hardness.
pass_b: We answer: the will to harden Paul names there designates a peculiar act of the divine will by which he denies certain persons that singular grace by which their hearts would be softened. God, as Augustine truly says, does not harden by imparting malice, but by not imparting mercy — as the setting sun, drawing back its rays, is said to darken the air not by an influx that begets darkness, but by denying the influx whose presence would remove the dark. Since this hardening is done by permitting and denying special mercy, no one can be considered and foresighted by God as finally hardened in sin and dying unless the decree of that permissive hardening — or that denial of special mercy — precedes, by which God knows final remaining in sin would be blocked if the mercy were granted. So the argument's assumption — that this hardening will (which is reprobation) presupposes the reprobate's sins as cause of that reprobation or hardening — is not only false but alien to reason and common sense. Cause precedes effect: yet the reprobate's final remaining in sin follows the decree of not-having-mercy or of hardening. If God has mercy, man is not hardened; that special mercy's work is to soften. So Augustine: If God willed to have mercy on them, he could so call (as apt for them) that they would be moved, understand, and follow. A little later: God has mercy on no one in vain. At length: God's hardening is nothing but not willing to have mercy — namely by withholding the grace that infallibly and efficaciously softens and converts. Since no final obstinacy in contracted or committed sins can be supposed unless God's will not to soften precedes it, foresighted perseverance of the reprobate in their sins cannot be the cause of that denied mercy or softening. True: in daily life the reprobate, by quenching the light God kindles in their hearts, repelling divine motions, and basely obeying foul lusts, merit consequent blinding, desertion, and handing over to a reprobate mind. But under all that stands the divine permission — or denial of special grace — which may be called permissive hardening and flows from reprobation. Without that going before, and depending on God's freest will, the reprobate would not have fallen into that final contumacy, but by special unowed mercy would have been freed from that rebellion and hardness.

lemmas.gloss: hardening = not willing to have mercy
